# Glossa Lab — Privacy and Data-Handling Statement

## 1. What this statement covers

Glossa Lab is a research workbench: a program for testing claims
about the Indus script, claim by claim, against the evidence. It
comes in two editions that are two doors into the same program:

- **The desktop edition** runs on one person's own computer. That
  person is the operator, and everything the program holds sits on
  that computer.
- **The cloud edition**, at glossa.bitconcepts.tech, lets invited
  members sign in through a website and use the same program, which
  still runs on the owner's desktop computer.

This statement says, for each edition, what information the system
holds, where it sits, when anything leaves the machine it sits on,
and what choices the people involved have. Words we cannot avoid
are explained the first time they appear.

## 2. The desktop edition: your work stays on your computer

### Where your work is stored

Everything the desktop edition holds — the research database, the
corpora and files you load, the claims, anchor sets, jobs, and
reports you create, and the program's settings — is stored in one
data folder on your own computer (on Windows, under your local
application data, in `GlossaLab\data`). The database is a single
file in that folder. Nothing in the desktop edition stores your
work on anyone else's computer.

### The install token

The program's interface and its data are guarded by one **token**:
a long random password the program creates for itself the first
time it runs. The token is kept in a small file inside the data
folder, set so only your operating-system account can read it
(file mode 0600 on systems that support it). Anything that talks
to the program — the app window, the tray, the command-line tools —
must present this token; anything that does not gets a refusal.
The token is never sent to us or to anyone else, it is never shown
in full on any screen (screens show only a short fingerprint, the
first characters of its checksum), and it can be replaced at any
time with the program's rotate command, which takes effect
immediately. A short health readout is the only thing the program
answers without the token, and it contains no research data.

### Keys you type into Settings

You can give the program keys for outside services — for example an
AI provider such as Mistral, OpenAI, Anthropic, or Google, scholarly
search services, or an email account for notifications. Those keys
are stored in a file named `.keys.json` inside the data folder,
separate from the database. Two honest details:

- The file is **not encrypted**. It is protected by the same
  restricted file permissions as the token file, and by your
  operating-system account — anyone who can read your files as you
  can read this file.
- The program never shows a stored key back. Its settings screens
  report only whether a key is set, never the key itself.

Leaving a key out is always an option: the parts of the program
that need a key simply stay off, and nothing fails because a key is
missing.

### The only times anything leaves your computer

The desktop edition has no reporting of its own — no usage
statistics, no crash reports, no check-ins with us. Data leaves
your computer only when you use a feature that needs an outside
service, and only to that service:

- **AI features.** When you run a feature that asks an AI service
  to read or draft text, the text you submit is sent to the
  provider you configured, under your own account and key, and the
  provider's own terms govern what it does with it.
- **Scholarly sources.** The program searches and fetches public
  research sources (for example Crossref, CORE, and GDELT) and
  downloads what you ask it to. Your search terms go to those
  services as part of the search.
- **Email you configure.** If you set up the email settings, the
  program sends the notices you asked for — a discovery digest and
  completion notices for studies and experiments — from your mail
  account to the addresses you configured. If the email settings
  are blank, it sends nothing.

### Copies and backups

Any copy of your data folder or database — a backup, a snapshot,
an export — exists only because you or your tools made it, and it
lives wherever you put it. The program makes no copies of your
work anywhere else.

## 3. The cloud edition: a members-only door to the same desktop

The cloud edition does not move the program. The research data
stays on the owner's desktop computer, in the same install the
owner uses locally. The website is a gate and a passageway in
front of it, run on Cloudflare (a hosting provider). Only people
with an account may sign in and use it; there is no public access
and no self-service sign-up — every account begins as an invitation
from an administrator, or as the single administrator account
created when the deployment was set up.

### What the website holds

The website's own database (Cloudflare D1) holds **identity data
only**:

- **Accounts**: a username, an email address if one is on record,
  the account's global type (owner, admin, member, or guest), its
  status, and when it was created, disabled, or removed.
- **Password hashes** — see below.
- **Invitations**: who created the invitation, the email address it
  was issued to (when it is bound to one), the workspace access it
  carries, and its expiry, revocation, and redemption state.
- **Sessions**: a record for each sign-in, with its creation, last
  activity, and expiry times.
- **Workspaces and access**: the list of workspaces (the program's
  projects, carried under that name) and, for each person, the role
  they hold in each workspace.
- **Setup state**: whether the one-time administrator setup has
  been completed.
- **The audit log** — see below.

That is the whole list. **The research dataset is never copied to
the website's storage, or to any other cloud storage.** There is
no cloud copy to browse, back up, or leak. When the desktop
computer is off or the program is stopped, the website answers
with a plain "the host is offline" message and nothing else — it
has no project data of its own to serve.

### Passwords and one-time codes

- Passwords are stored only as **hashes** — a one-way scrambled
  form (produced with Argon2id, a password-hashing method designed
  to be slow to guess) from which the password cannot be read back.
  Nobody, including an administrator, can see your password.
- Invitation codes, session tokens, and the one-time setup code
  are likewise stored only as hashes (SHA-256). The readable code
  exists only in the invitation itself and in your browser.
- There is **no password recovery by email** in this edition. If
  you lose your password, an administrator disables the account
  and issues a fresh invitation; that is the designed way back in.

### Staying signed in

Signing in sets one cookie in your browser (a small marker the
website uses to recognize your session). It is marked so scripts
cannot read it and so it travels only over encrypted connections,
and it lasts up to 30 days. You can see and revoke your sessions
from your account page. Changing your password ends every other
session and keeps only the one you are using. An administrator
can revoke a session or disable an account at any time, and a
disabled account cannot sign in.

### The audit log

The website keeps an **audit log**: an append-only list of
security-relevant events — sign-ins and failed sign-ins,
invitations created, redeemed, and revoked, password changes,
session revocations, account disabling and removal, and the
completion of the one-time setup. Append-only is enforced by the
database itself, not just by convention: the log's rows cannot be
edited or deleted through the database. The log records *that*
the setup was completed — never the setup code, and never any
password.

If an account is removed, the account is closed and its sessions
are deleted, but the person's name stays attached to the work
they already did and to their past entries in the audit log. That
is deliberate: the record of who did what is part of the research
record.

### How long identity records are kept

Expired invitations and audit-log entries are retained for
12 months. That period is the owner's policy default, set when
this statement was approved, and the owner can change it by a
recorded decision. It is a policy, not an automated process:
nothing in the current build removes old entries on its own, and
the audit log's append-only construction means applying the
period to audit entries is an operator act under the owner's
direction.

### Workspaces: who can see what

Work is organized into workspaces, and access is decided **per
workspace**. A person can hold a different role — owner, admin,
member, or viewer — in each workspace they belong to. Guests are
never more than viewers anywhere. You are shown only the
workspaces you belong to; a workspace you have no access to does
not appear in your lists, counts, or search results, not even as
a name. If you ask for something outside your access, the answer
is the same "not found" you would get if it did not exist.
A workspace that has been archived serves nothing to anyone.

### How requests reach the desktop

Your requests reach the program on the desktop only after you
have signed in, and only for the parts of the program your access
covers. The website removes any identity labels a visitor's
browser attaches to a request and adds its own only after
checking your session, together with a per-deployment **service
credential** (a secret shared between the website and the desktop
program) that proves the request really came through the website.
The desktop program's own install token (§2) plays no part here:
the website refuses it in every position, and it is never a
browser credential. The connection between the website and the
desktop runs over a private tunnel whose secret lives only in a
service configuration on the desktop — never in the program's
code, records, or this statement.

Features in the hosted app that call an AI service use the
service and key configured on the host desktop (§2). Text you
submit to those features is therefore sent to that provider,
under the host's account.

### Search engines

The hosted site is closed to search engines and indexing on
purpose: its robots file tells crawlers to stay away from every
page, and every response carries a "noindex" instruction. That
posture stays until the owner decides to lift it.

### The hosting provider

The gate described above runs on Cloudflare's network, so
Cloudflare necessarily handles the traffic between your browser
and the desktop. What Cloudflare itself records in its own
operational systems, and how long it keeps it, is governed by
Cloudflare's own terms and is not something this codebase
controls or describes. The Worker's own configuration, which is
part of this program's code, enables no logging or measurement
collection of its own; the one measurement service switched on
for this domain at the account level is Cloudflare Web
Analytics, described in §5.

## 4. The research material itself

The program works on other scholars' corpora, and those materials
carry their own rules, which the program follows:

- The primary corpus (the Holdat Indus Corpus) is proprietary.
  It is used for statistical analysis only. Its raw data is not
  committed to the program's code repository and is never
  released.
- Files derived from the Corpus of Indus Seals and Inscriptions
  (CISI) are reference material: used inside the research, not
  for redistribution.
- The program's custody rule, in its own words: **statistics
  publishable, scans never redistributed.** Restricted material —
  scans and what is derived from them — stays in restricted
  folders on the owner's own machines. Through the cloud edition
  it can be returned only inside a signed-in session, to a member
  whose workspace access covers it, and under the same
  restrictions the desktop application already enforces. Hosting
  changes where the application runs; it does not widen what any
  member is allowed to receive.

What the program publishes is its own analysis: the preprint and
its statistics (released under CC BY 4.0), and the public research
tracker. The published readings are candidates, held to the
program's standing position:

> "The Indus script is not deciphered. The readings this program
> records are candidate readings, each one a claim standing at a
> stage of the claim lifecycle. A reading is not settled by being
> recorded and checked, and no count in this program is a measure
> of decipherment."

## 5. What we do not do

- We do not sell personal information, and no part of either
  edition sends member or research data to advertisers or data
  brokers.
- The desktop edition contains no analytics or telemetry: it
  reports nothing about your use to anyone (§2).
- Web analytics **is** switched on for this domain at the hosting
  account level. Cloudflare Web Analytics is enabled for
  bitconcepts.tech with automatic installation, and its
  configuration carries no exclusion for this site, so it
  applies here as it does across the domain (checked against the
  hosting account on 2026-11-05). It is Cloudflare's page-visit
  measurement, run under Cloudflare's own terms; it measures
  visits to pages and is not connected to the research dataset.

## 6. Your controls

- **Your account.** From your account page you can change your
  email address and your password, and see and revoke your
  sessions.
- **Closing an account.** Ask an administrator to disable or
  remove your account. Disabling stops sign-in immediately.
  Removal closes the account and deletes its sessions; as §3
  explains, your name remains on work you already did and in the
  audit log.
- **Exporting your work.** You can export your own work from a
  workspace. A project exports as a single JSON bundle holding
  the project and the work linked to it (hypotheses, notebooks,
  citations, and correspondence). Reports you generate can be
  downloaded as files, and corpus texts can be exported in text,
  CSV, or JSON form. An export is a copy — it removes nothing —
  and it reaches only the workspaces your access covers, under
  the same rule as §3: a workspace you cannot see cannot be
  exported by you.

## 7. How this statement changes

Once approved, this text is kept as the single approved version
under the program's policy-sync rules. It changes only through a
recorded approval by the owner of the new text, and the copy the
system serves is checked against the approved version
automatically, so the served words and the approved words cannot
quietly drift apart.

*Version: 1.0 — approved by the owner on 2026-11-05, effective
from that date. This is the first approved version; the version
history begins here.*

## 8. Questions

Questions about this statement, or about how the program handles
your data, can be sent to tristen@bitconcepts.tech.
